noteBlocks.lede: A matrix equation is solved the way any equation is: undo what was done to the unknown matrix. An added or subtracted matrix is undone entry by entry. A matrix that multiplies cannot be divided away, so its inverse does the undoing, written in front on both sides.
can: Solve $A + X = B$ and $A - X = B$ entry by entry, in the right direction.
Solve $AX = B$ as $X = A^{-1}B$, the inverse in front, whatever the determinant.
Clear an added matrix first, and say why a singular matrix stops the method.

noteBlocks.text: Undo what was done to X

noteBlocks.md: A matrix equation is solved like a number equation: do the same to both sides until $X$ is alone. An added matrix is taken away from both sides, position by position, and the direction matters: $A + X = B$ gives $X = B - A$, never $A - B$. From $A - X = B$, add $X$ to both sides first: $X = A - B$.

noteBlocks.stem: It is given that $A + X = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 1 & 7\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Take $A$ from both sides; what is left on the right is $B - A$.
Each entry of $A$ comes off the entry in the same place in $B$.
Check: $A + X$ gives $B$ back.

noteBlocks.prompt: It is given that $X + A = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 \\ -2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. Which matrix is $X$?
noteBlocks.explain: Take $A$ from both sides, as step 1 of See it did, so $X = B - A$, worked position by position: top left $6 - 1 = 5$. $A - B$ reverses every sign, and $A + B$ adds where the equation needs taking away.

twin.prompt: It is given that $X + A = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Which matrix is $X$?
twin.explain: $X = B - A$, position by position: top left $4 - 3 = 1$, top right $1 - (-2) = 3$.

optionNotes.why: That reverses every sign: the rearrangement gives B − A.
That adds A on, where it has to come off.
That is $A - B$: taking $A$ from both sides leaves $B - A$, so every sign here is reversed.
That adds $A$ on, where the equation needs it taken off.

noteBlocks.text: When A multiplies X, use the inverse

noteBlocks.md: In $AX = B$ the matrix $A$ multiplies $X$, and there is no dividing by a matrix. What undoes $A$ is its inverse: $A^{-1}A = I$, the identity, which acts like the number $1$. So multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$, and $X$ is left on its own.

noteBlocks.title: Why there is no dividing by a matrix
noteBlocks.md: For numbers, dividing by $4$ is multiplying by $\frac{1}{4}$, the number that undoes $4$. A matrix has no reciprocal, but it may have an inverse that does the same job, and only when its determinant is not zero. So the undo is multiplication by $A^{-1}$.

steps.decision: Multiply both sides by the inverse, written in front of each side.
A matrix times its own inverse is the identity matrix, $I$.
The identity changes nothing it multiplies, so $IX$ is simply $X$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Multiplying both sides of $AX = B$ by $A^{-1}$ gives $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$. What happened to $A^{-1}A$ on the way to $X = A^{-1}B$?
options: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
noteBlocks.answer: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
noteBlocks.explain: Step 2 of See it: a matrix times its own inverse is the identity, the matrix version of $1$, and step 3 used $IX = X$. It does not vanish to zero, and it is not $A$ times itself.

twin.prompt: Which matrix, multiplied in front of $LX$, leaves $X$ on its own?
twin.explain: $L^{-1}L = I$ and $IX = X$. $L$ itself would give $L^{2}X$, and there is no dividing by a matrix.

optionNotes.why: $L$ in front gives $L^{2}X$; only the inverse undoes $L$.
There is no dividing by a matrix; its inverse does that job.
A matrix times its own inverse is the identity, not the zero matrix; zero would wipe X out.
$A^{-1}A$ is the inverse times the matrix, not $A$ times $A$: the inverse undoes $A$.

noteBlocks.md: The inverse goes in front of $A$, where it meets $A$ and makes $I$, so it goes in front of $B$ as well: the same thing, in the same place, on both sides. The place matters because two matrices multiplied the other way round usually give a different matrix, so $BA^{-1}$ is not the answer.

steps.decision: Row by column, with the inverse first.
The same two matrices the other way round: a different matrix.

noteBlocks.prompt: To solve $LX = M$ for $X$, where must $L^{-1}$ be written?
options: In front of the left side only
noteBlocks.explain: In front of $L$, so that $L^{-1}L$ becomes $I$, and in the same place on the right to keep the sides equal, which is the product step 3 of See it checked: $X = L^{-1}M$. Behind $L$ the inverse never meets it, so $X$ is never freed.

twin.prompt: Multiplying both sides of $LX = M$ by $L^{-1}$, which product is $X$?
twin.explain: The inverse goes in front on both sides, so the right side becomes $L^{-1}M$. $ML^{-1}$ is the other order, usually a different matrix.

optionNotes.why: That is the other order, usually a different matrix: the inverse goes in front.
One inverse in front of each side is all it takes; nothing multiplies on the right.
Behind $L$ the inverse never meets it, so $L^{-1}L$ is never formed and $X$ is not freed.

optionNotes.option: In front of the left side only
optionNotes.why: Whatever is done to one side is done to the other, in the same place, or the equation breaks.

steps.decision: The determinant first, on its own line; it is not zero, so the inverse exists.

noteBlocks.title: Matrix Equations part 1 - Corbettmaths
noteBlocks.why: The same method on several equations, the inverse written in front each time, beside our own steps above.

noteBlocks.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 to 4 of See it: $\det A = 9 - 8 = 1$, so $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1 times the column: $3 \times 5 + (-2) \times 6 = 3$.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?

noteBlocks.md: Most papers set an inverse with a fraction in front, often a negative one: $\det A = -2$ gives $-\frac{1}{2}$. Keep that fraction outside the matrix. Multiply the swapped-and-negated matrix by $B$ first, in whole numbers, and divide by the determinant at the very end, minus sign included.

noteBlocks.stem: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Negative, so the fraction in front of the inverse is negative.
Swap, change two signs, and keep $-\frac{1}{2}$ outside.
Row by column in whole numbers: $4 \times 5 + (-3) \times 6 = 2$ and $-2 \times 5 + 1 \times 6 = -4$.
Now divide by $-2$: every sign flips. Check: $AX$ gives $B$.

noteBlocks.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$, as a decimal?
noteBlocks.explain: As steps 1 to 4 of See it: $\det A = 8 - 3 = 5$. Row 1 of the swapped-and-negated matrix times the column is $4 \times 1 + (-1) \times 1 = 3$, and dividing by $5$ last gives $\frac{3}{5} = 0.6$.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$, as a decimal?

noteBlocks.md: When the equation also adds or subtracts a matrix, clear that first, exactly as in a number equation: from $AX - C = B$, add $C$ to both sides to reach $AX = B + C$. Only then bring in the inverse, and let it multiply the whole of $B + C$. The papers have set this as $(P - Q)X = R$ and as $AX = B + C$.

noteBlocks.stem: It is given that $AX - C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $C = \begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Add $C$ to both sides first; $A$ waits.
Swap and change signs; the determinant is 1.
The inverse multiplies the whole right side, bracket and all.
Row by column. Check: $AX - C$ gives $B$.

noteBlocks.prompt: It is given that $AX + C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?
noteBlocks.explain: Clear $C$ first, as step 1 of See it did: $AX = B - C = \begin{pmatrix}6 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, and row 1 gives $18 - 8 = 10$. Going straight to $A^{-1}B$ solves a different equation.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX - C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}6 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?

noteBlocks.md: **No inverse.** If the matrix multiplying $X$ has determinant $0$, it has no inverse and the equation cannot be solved this way. Say so naming the matrix: in 2023 some answers only said the matrix had no inverse, without saying which. A part may instead ask which value makes a matrix singular (2021).
**Unknown entries.** A product with letters in it (2021, 2024): multiply it out row by column, then set the matching entries equal and solve.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new method, so answer from what you already know.
What is the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 7 & 2\end{pmatrix}$?

options.feedback: The determinant is $8 - 7 = 1$, so swapping the leading diagonal and changing the other two signs is the whole of it.
Every sign has been changed. Only the other diagonal changes sign.
The signs changed but the leading diagonal never swapped.
Take $7$ from both sides. A matrix equation with an added matrix works the same way.
The $7$ has been added rather than taken away.
The $7$ is added to $x$, not multiplying it, so division does not undo it.

items.stem: For two matrices $P$ and $Q$, is $PQ$ always the same as $QP$?

options.text: No, the order changes the product
options.feedback: That is why an inverse has to be written on the same side of both sides of an equation.

options.text: Yes, multiplication can be done in any order
options.feedback: That holds for numbers. Matrix products depend on the order, and often only one of the two exists.
Even two square matrices of the same size usually give different products in the two orders.

items.stem: An equation reads $A + X = B$. What is $X$?

options.feedback: Take $A$ from both sides, entry by entry.
The subtraction is the wrong way round, so every entry has the opposite sign.
$A$ is added here, not multiplying, so no inverse is needed.

items.stem: An equation reads $AX = B$. What is $X$?

options.feedback: The inverse goes in front of both sides, so $A^{-1}A$ becomes the identity.
That is the inverse behind $B$. Because the order changes a product, it gives a different matrix.
Division is not defined for matrices. The inverse is what replaces it.

items.stem: Which of these is $X$ for $AX = B$, with $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$?
items.skill: Working the product in the right order

options.feedback: $A^{-1}B$, with the inverse in front: $\det A = 1$ and $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
That is $BA^{-1}$, the inverse behind $B$; the order changes the product.
That is $AB$: the matrix itself was used where its inverse belonged.

items.stem: An equation reads $AX + C = B$. What is the first step?
items.skill: The order of operations in a combined equation

options.feedback: Clear the added matrix first; only then does the inverse come in.

options.text: Multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$ straight away
options.feedback: That leaves $C$ inside the equation and solves a different one.
$A$ is multiplying $X$, so subtracting it undoes nothing.

items.stem: The matrix $S = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Can the equation $SX = B$ be solved?

options.text: No, because $\det S = 0$ and $S$ has no inverse
options.feedback: Without an inverse there is nothing to pre-multiply by, so the equation has no single solution.

options.text: Yes, by dividing both sides by $S$
options.feedback: Matrices are never divided, and this one has no inverse either.
Being square is not enough. The determinant has to be something other than zero.

parts.stem:
It is given that $A + X = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the matrix $X$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Take $A$ from both sides.
Subtract entry by entry.
parts.workedSolution:
Taking $A$ from both sides gives $X = B - A$.
Entry by entry, $X = \begin{pmatrix}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $A - B$. Taking $A$ from both sides leaves $B - A$, so every entry has the opposite sign: $\begin{pmatrix}5 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solutionProgram: main: Taking $A$ from both sides gives $X = B - A$. Entry by entry, $X = \begin{pmatrix}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
It is given that $A - X = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 1 & 7\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the matrix $X$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Here it is $X$ that is being taken away, so move it across first.
parts.workedSolution:
From $A - X = B$, adding $X$ to both sides gives $A = B + X$, so $X = A - B$.
Entry by entry, $X = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 1 & 7\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -3 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $B - A$. Because $X$ was the one being subtracted, the rearrangement gives $X = A - B$, which is $\begin{pmatrix}4 & -3 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solutionProgram: main: From $A - X = B$, adding $X$ to both sides gives $A = B + X$, so $X = A - B$. Entry by entry, $X = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 1 & 7\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -3 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}10 \\ 20\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the matrix $X$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: The determinant is not $1$ here, so the inverse carries a fraction.
Keep the fraction with every entry.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det A = 10$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
$X = A^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}10 \\ 20\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$.
Checking, $AX = \begin{pmatrix}10 \\ 20\end{pmatrix}$, which is $B$.

commonErrors.feedback: The swapped and negated matrix was used without dividing by the determinant, so every entry is $10$ times too big. With the division, $X = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$.

It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the matrix $X$.

parts.stem:
It is given that $AX + C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}11 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$.
Find the matrix $X$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Clear $C$ first.
Only then bring in the inverse.
parts.workedSolution:
Taking $C$ from both sides: $AX = B - C = \begin{pmatrix}8 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$.
$\det A = 1$, so $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
$X = A^{-1}(B - C) = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}8 \\ 3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-5 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$.
Checking, $AX + C = \begin{pmatrix}11 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$, which is $B$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $A^{-1}B$: the inverse was applied with $C$ still in the equation. Clearing $C$ first gives $AX = \begin{pmatrix}8 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$, and then $X = \begin{pmatrix}-5 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
It is given that $P = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, $Q = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $R = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$.
Find $P - Q$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Subtract position by position: each entry of $Q$ from the entry in the same place in $P$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $Q - P$: every sign is reversed. $P - Q$ takes each entry of $Q$ from $P$: $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
Find $(P - Q)^{-1}$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: The determinant first.
Swap the leading diagonal, change the other two signs, divide by the determinant.

commonErrors.feedback: The swapped-and-negated matrix is right; it still has to be divided by the determinant: $(P - Q)^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:

Write the answer as a matrix.

scheme.for: $X = (P - Q)^{-1}R$, with the inverse in front
the product worked row by column

hints: The inverse from part (b) goes in front of $R$.
Keep the $\frac{1}{7}$ outside until the end.

$X = \frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}$.
Checking, $(P - Q)X = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked to find $X$ for $LX = M$, where $L = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $M = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right: the determinant and the inverse are correct. Line 3 puts the inverse behind M. Multiplying both sides by the inverse puts it in front of each side, so X is L inverse times M, and because the order of a product changes the answer, line 4 is accurate arithmetic on the wrong product. X should be (3 5 ; -5 -8).
findTheMistake.feedback: Write the inverse in front of both sides on one line, before any multiplying: L inverse L X = L inverse M. Then the order is settled before the arithmetic starts.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara needs $B^{2}$ on the way to solving $AY = B^{2}$, where $B = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 squares each entry. B² means B times B, worked row by column, so the top-left entry is 3 × 3 + 1 × 2 = 11, not 3² = 9. B² = (11 2 ; 4 3), and Y is then found from that matrix.
findTheMistake.feedback: A power of a matrix is repeated multiplication: write B² as B times B, then work each entry as a row times a column.

prompts.prompt: How do you solve $A + X = B$?
prompts.answer: Take $A$ from both sides: $X = B - A$, worked entry by entry, in that direction.

prompts.prompt: Why can you not divide both sides of $AX = B$ by $A$?
prompts.answer: Division is not defined for matrices. What replaces it is multiplying by the inverse, which exists when the determinant is not zero.
$X = A^{-1}B$, with the inverse in front of $B$.

prompts.prompt: Give the three lines that justify $X = A^{-1}B$.
prompts.answer: $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$; $A^{-1}A$ is the identity, so $IX = A^{-1}B$; the identity leaves $X$ unchanged, so $X = A^{-1}B$.

prompts.prompt: What is the first step for $AX + C = B$?
prompts.answer: Take $C$ from both sides, giving $AX = B - C$. The inverse comes in only after the added matrix is cleared.

prompts.prompt: $A$ is $2 \times 2$ and $B$ is $2 \times 1$. What shape is $X$ in $AX = B$?
prompts.answer: A $2 \times 1$ column: as many rows as $A$ and as many columns as $B$.

prompts.prompt: An equation is $SX = B$ and $\det S = 0$. What do you write?
prompts.answer: That $S$ has no inverse because its determinant is zero, so the equation cannot be solved. Name the matrix, not just the determinant.

prompts.prompt: Where does the inverse go when you solve $AX = B$?
prompts.answer: In front of both sides, so $X = A^{-1}B$.
